rationale: B wins because it is a little harsher about what can actually be verified. Its angle, "Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see," turns Glossier's private-company opacity into real reporting tension; A's "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is clean, but closer to a profile frame that needs access and history the update does not provide. Both sets are usable; B asks the sharper first-reply questions before the founder can get comfortable.
gaps_in_A: "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" risks becoming a company-profile wrapper unless Glossier supplies principal access and actual inflection points. The update gives a blog origin, not a profile package.
"cult brand's positioning" imports brand-color that was not in the update. It may be true in the real world; it is not grounded in the supplied facts.

"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" depends heavily on how many of the 800 new doors are actually Sephora at Kohl's. A catches this in proof needs, but the headline is too confident before that split is known.
gaps_in_B: "suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora" is a geography and shopper assumption smuggled in from "Sephora at Kohl's." Useful instinct, but not a supplied fact.

"one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" and "the whole generation of internet-native brands" need outside comparisons. B names the proof need, but the angle is already leaning on the cohort frame.

The door-count angle and "Sephora is betting more shelf" may collide in the same retail-trade inbox. One counts the space; the other interrogates Sephora's bet, but they need tighter separation in execution.
